newsitem.title: HUNGARY: POWERGEN HUNGARY DEAL MODEL FOR FUTURE-MVM.
newsitem.headline: POWERGEN HUNGARY DEAL MODEL FOR FUTURE-MVM.

text.p: Hungarian electricity supply company MVM said the long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) it signed with British generator Powergen Plc would serve as model for forthcoming tenders for new plants.
"This PPA will be the standard for the new capacities," MVM's strategic director Istvan Bakacs told Reuters.

Powergen, the first foreign investor to secure such an agreement in Hungary, said on Monday that its subsidiary Csepel Aramtermelo Rt had signed a 20-year contract with MVM, paving the way for the development of a $261 million power plant in Budapest.
MVM said on Monday it planned to invite two tenders in July for the construction of 2000 megawatts of new Hungarian capacity.
The first tender will be for smaller capacity units of 20 to 200 MW for commissioning beween 2001 and 2003 while the second will be for larger plants to go on line between 2003 and 2005.
"This standardised formula (used in the agreement with Powergen) will be attached to the tendering as well," Bakacs said.

German consortium RWE Energie AG and EVS AG announced on Monday it would participate in the second tender with a plan to build two new lignite-powered 500 MW power plants at Bukkabrany, part of the Matra power plant site it runs in north-east Hungary.
But it indicated the investment depended on resolving current drawn-out talks on energy prices and on securing a PPA with MVM.

Bakacs told Reuters the agreement with Powergen had taken five months to negotiate as it was the first PPA to include a long-term automatic formula taking into account factors such as forint depreciation and world prices.
"Before, (power purchases) were related to government price-settings," he said. "Here we have committed ourselves for 20 years under the formula -- that is the most major issue, I believe."
He said the agreement also included some termination and forces majeurs clauses but said the formula would only be applied to new or substantially refurbished power plants.

As well as RWE-EVS's coal-fired Matra power station, other plants with large foreign investments are the oil-fired Dunamenti plant, in central Hungary, run by Tractebel of Belgium, and Tisza, in the east, operated by AES of the U.S.

Tractebel has complained that the price it receives for its power does not ensure the eight percent profit margin all foreign investors were promised when they bought into the sector in 1995 and 1996.
"We don't want to change the PPA with the existing power stations," Bakacs said.

"But if (Tractebel) commit themselves to major refurbishments of the existing plant such as a substantial time/life extension, retrofitting to the environmental regulations or adding new capacity, it could lead to a new PPA," Bakacs said.
The RWE-EVS consortium signed a 47 billion forint deal with the Hungarian government on Monday on retrofitting three 200 MW coal-fired units at the Matra site.
